Event Description mention clearly and el:
Event Title: 60 Seconds: Chemical Apocalypse

Theme: Chemical Safety, Emergency Response, and Industrial Filtration

Event Overview
60 Seconds: Chemical Apocalypse is an intense, hands-on simulation where students step into the shoes of an emergency disaster response team. Following a sudden chemical leak at a plant, teams must think fast, manage limited resources, and solve real-world engineering problems under tight time pressure.

Starting with a fast-paced, 60-second material scramble, teams must build functional protection gear, stop chemical leaks, trade resources with rival teams, and spot fraudulent safety credentials—all using only the tools they manage to scavenge.

Core Engineering Concepts Covered
Chemical Adsorption & Filtration: Students learn why basic cloth fails against chemical vapors, seeing firsthand how activated charcoal actively traps toxic fumes at a microscopic level.
Airflow & Filter Design: Teams learn to balance filter density—making sure a mask is thick enough to catch toxins, but breathable enough for air to pass through.
Process Control & Isolation: Teams must identify and operate emergency shutdown valves to isolate leaking pipe sections, balancing system pressure changes to safely stop chemical releases at the source.
Industrial Safety Protocols: Solutions are judged on real industrial safety standards, teaching participants how real chemical engineers handle dangerous spills, toxic gases, and emergency gear ratings.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
Team Setup & Rules
Team Size: 2 to 5 participants per team.

The Designated Runner: Each team nominates one designated runner to enter the supply zone during the scramble.

Carrying Capacity Rule: The runner can carry a maximum of two items at a time (one in each hand). No bags, pockets, or extra containers may be used during the scramble.

Property Lock: Once the 60-second scramble ends, all collected items become the permanent property of that team for the remainder of the event, forming their sole survival inventory.

Phase-by-Phase Gameplay
Phase 1: The 60-Second Scramble
The Setup: A shared central table contains a limited pool of safety gear, laboratory tools, raw materials, and structural items.

The Action: At the sound of the emergency siren, the designated runner from each team enters the supply zone simultaneously.

The Scramble: The runner has 60 seconds to inspect the available inventory, select up to two items, run back to their team station to drop them off, and dash back to collect more. Teams must continuously communicate from their stations to tell their runner which specific items to prioritize before time expires.

Phase 2: Crisis Management & Problem Solving (Rounds 1–4)
Teams face sequential emergency scenario rounds representing escalating challenges within a breached chemical facility (e.g., acid spills, volatile gas leaks, structural breaches, or toxic runoff).

Teams must formulate and write down practical engineering solutions or fabricate physical functional setups using only the items in their inventory.

Phase 3: Internal Trading Window (Stage 5)
Duration: Exactly 60 seconds.

Mechanic: Teams enter an open negotiation market where they can barter and trade items directly with rival teams. A team lacking charcoal for gas filtration might trade excess duct tape or plastic equipment to another team in need of structural materials.

Phase 4: Advanced Scenarios & The External Visitor (Rounds 6–8+)
Crisis Progression: Scenarios become more complex, requiring multi-layered solutions (e.g., combined filtration, neutralization, and structural sealing).

The External Visitor Event (After Round 8): An unknown outside survivor/trader arrives at the facility offering a high-value trade proposition (e.g., trading rare filtration components for vital safety gear).

The Verification Challenge: Teams must analyze the visitor’s technical pitch, credentials, and offered materials to determine if they are genuine or a fraudulent imposter. Making a trade with a fake visitor results in losing valuable inventory for useless or compromised materials

Event Description mention clearly and el:
This proposed event is a structured, zero-contact 3v3 laser tag tournament designed for efficient participant turnover, clear operational boundaries, and strict safety compliance. Matches are played in strictly timed 5-to-10-minute rounds within a custom-built, temporary arena featuring fixed physical barriers and defensive cover points. The tournament utilizes a dynamic, multi-layered scoring system: teams earn base points for eliminating opponents and receive time-remaining bonus multipliers for quick squad eliminations, but face strict point deductions for every verified electronic hit they sustain. To further elevate the game's complexity, an interactive retrieval mechanic is integrated. Hidden objects are strategically scattered throughout the arena, allowing players to earn significant bonus points by successfully locating them while actively evading enemy fire. All match data is continuously tracked on a centralized leaderboard to determine overall tournament standings.

To ensure dynamic gameplay and complete operational control, strict arena rules are enforced by dedicated referees. All physical obstacles are strictly stationary; players cannot move, alter, or climb them, nor can they use them to physically block opponents. Gameplay mechanics require a clear line of sight for all valid hits, explicitly prohibiting blind firing around corners or shooting through structural gaps. Additionally, an anti-camping protocol mandates that players cannot remain behind a single obstacle for more than 30 seconds without moving, which naturally encourages continuous exploration for the hidden objects. Because the event relies entirely on non-projectile electronic blasters and wearable sensors, it carries zero physical or projectile risks, guaranteeing a highly controlled and safe environment for the venue.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
1. Obstacles are fixed: Players cannot move, rotate, climb, or remove any obstacle.
2. Cover can be used for defence: Players are allowed to hide completely behind an obstacle, peek from the side/top to aim, and move between obstacles.
3. No shooting through obstacles: A hit counts only when the gun has a clear line of sight to the opponent’s sensor/hit zone.
4. No blind shooting: Players shouldn’t shoot around a corner without being able to see where they’re aiming.
5. No excessive camping: A player cannot remain behind the same obstacle for more than 20–30 seconds without moving.
6. No physical interaction with cover: Don’t push an obstacle, block another player's movement, climb on top of obstacles, or hurt/push anyone physically.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
SDC Games is a two-day, multi-domain technical and non-technical competition organized by the Software Development Club (SDC) as part of Technozion 2026. The event is designed to test participants across different areas of technology while also incorporating elements of creativity, problem-solving, teamwork, strategy, and observation.

The event consists of four technical domains - AI/ML, Coding, Cyber Security, and Web Development, and two non-technical domains: Design and PR.

Day 1 – Multi-Domain Challenge

Day 1 consists of four rounds. Three rounds are technical and are conducted in parallel by the four technical wings, while the third round is a common fun and entertainment round conducted jointly by the Design and PR teams.

For each technical round, participants can choose any one of the four technical domains according to their interest and attempt the challenge conducted by that domain. However, a participant cannot choose the same technical domain more than once across the technical rounds of Day 1. This allows participants to explore different domains and compete in multiple areas.

The technical challenges are designed with increasing levels of difficulty, with each subsequent challenge within a domain being more advanced than its preceding level. The technical rounds include quizzes, debugging, reverse coding, web development challenges, cybersecurity challenges, OSINT-based tasks, AI/ML puzzles, and location-based problem-solving activities.

The third round is a non-technical fun round, jointly conducted by the Design and PR teams, and is intended to provide a break from the technical challenges while testing participants through an engaging and interactive activity.

Participants' performance across the Day 1 rounds will contribute to their cumulative score. Based on the overall cumulative performance, participants will be shortlisted for the Day 2 challenges.

Day 2 – Common Cross-Domain Challenge

Day 2 brings the shortlisted participants together for common challenges that combine multiple technical domains. Instead of competing within a single domain, participants will be required to apply knowledge from different areas such as AI/ML, Web Development, Coding, Cyber Security, logic, observation, and teamwork.

The proposed Day 2 challenges are designed as immersive, scenario-based competitions where participants must solve interconnected problems, make strategic decisions, collaborate with teammates, and apply concepts from multiple technical domains to progress through the challenge.

Overall, SDC Games aims to provide participants with a unique competitive experience where they are not restricted to a single technical domain. The event combines technical knowledge with creativity, logical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, strategy, and real-world application, making it an engaging multi-domain competition for Technozion 2026.

Ever wanted to be a hacker? Break into enemy systems, seize control, and claim what's not yours — all while keeping your own turf safe from everyone trying to do the same to you. DEFCON 2.0 is HAM ARC's live attack-and-defense hacking hackathon, a full-scale cyber battleground where teams go head-to-head over real machines, real vulnerabilities, and real consequences. This isn't a simulation or a slideshow — it's hands-on, live, and happening right in front of you.

Every team gets a machine to defend and a battlefield of rivals to hunt. The mission is simple: find their weaknesses before they find yours, break in first, and take control — all while making sure your own machine doesn't fall to the team gunning for you. It's a constant push and pull between offense and defense, and the team that plays it best walks away as the top hacking crew on campus. Cash prize: ₹10,000.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
Rules of the Event

Format & Rounds
1. Round 1 — Fortify: Teams receive their assigned machine and a fixed window of time to inspect it, close obvious vulnerabilities, and shore up their defenses. No attacking is allowed during this round.
2. Round 2 — Attack: The arena goes live. All team machines are now visible and attackable on the network. Scan for weak or poorly-defended machines, break in, escalate access, and try to gain full control.
3. Round 3 — Reckoning: Final scoring and results based on how deep each team penetrated rival systems and how well they held their own.

Team Composition
- Teams of 1–4 members.
- Each team is given one attack workstation and one defended machine.

Core Rules
- Only attack machines belonging to opposing teams within the official arena network.
- No denial-of-service (DoS) attacks — crashing or flooding a machine is not allowed.
- Do not attack or interfere with another team's attack workstation.
- Compromise milestones (initial foothold, privilege escalation, full control) are automatically detected and scored.
- Sharing exploits, credentials, or access with other teams is not permitted.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
"EcoCity: Build to Last" is a sustainability-simulation game, where teams use a fixed budget to build a resilient city. The ultimate goal is long-term survival, not maximizing the budget spent; a lean, well-balanced city will outperform an overbuilt, resource-hungry one.
Game Mechanics
 * City Building: During a 30-minute build phase, teams purchase land, housing, agriculture, water facilities, and employment infrastructure via a built-in catalogue.
 * The Energy Trade-Off: Participants must balance cheap, highly polluting, and depletable coal against expensive, clean, and renewable wind or solar power.
 * Population: Population growth is automatic but strictly capped by the city's tightest resource whether that is housing, food, water, or jobs.
Simulation and Judging
 * The Engine: A deterministic, rule-based engine simulates the city year-by-year, tracking resource balances, coal reserves, and a pollution index.
 * Winning: The simulation stops if the city hits a resource deficit for consecutive years, crosses a pollution threshold, or if the population drops to zero. The longest-surviving city wins, capped at a 300-year "Sustainable" horizon.
 * Tie-Breakers: Ties are settled by the lowest peak pollution, followed by the lowest total spend.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou: 30-minute build phase using the provided web simulation tool. Deterministic engine scores max survival years (capped at 300 years). Ties broken by lowest peak pollution and lowest total budget spend.
